title: Start defining a new class with `class Card:` to contain card data and behavior

question: What does `class Card:` directly initiate?
explanation: 1) When you encounter the `class` keyword, you can tell that a new class definition is beginning. 2) The name “Card” that follows is the name of the class being defined. 3) The `__init__` and `is_correct` statements, indented below the colon, belong to the class body. 4) Once the `class` statement ends, the name “Card” refers to an instance of the class.
project_context: It is linked to a structure that groups related data and decision-making actions into a single model, similar to a learning card.
reading_goal_internal: class 헤더가 Card라는 새 클래스 객체의 정의를 시작하고 들여쓴 attribute 초기화와 method 정의가 그 클래스 본문에 속한다는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `class Name:` is a compound statement that defines a new class capable of encapsulating an object’s state and behavior.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the class name and the indentation boundaries of the body, and see which attributes and methods are defined within the body.
concept_explanation.key_point: While `class` is useful for grouping object models with related state and behavior, it is not strictly necessary in all code.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that a single Card instance is automatically created simply by defining the class.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Begin the definition of the `Sensor` class and include the instance initialization logic in the body.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) When you encounter the `class` keyword, you can tell that a new class definition is beginning. 2) The name “Card” that follows is the name of the class being defined. 3) The `__init__` and `is_correct` statements, indented below the colon, belong to the class body. 4) Once the `class` statement ends, the name “Card” refers to an instance of the class.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The `class` syntax begins a block that defines a class called `Card`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: An instance is created only after a separate class call, such as `Card(...)`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that a single Card instance is automatically created simply by defining the class.

title: Defining a simple calculation function directly using `def add(a, b):`
reading_goal: Read the function name `add` and its two positional parameters `a` and `b`, as well as the indented return block, and understand that this simple calculation is a structure expressed as a function without separate object state.
question: Which of the following is a correct explanation of `def add(a, b):`?
choices: Define a general function that takes a and b as arguments.
It is valid only within the class.
There is no `self`, so this is a syntax error.
answer: Define a general function that takes a and b as arguments.
explanation: 1) Identify that this is a function definition using the `def` keyword. 2) The function name is `add`. 3) The `a` and `b` inside the parentheses are the two parameters. 4) The indented `return` statement constitutes the body of the `add` function.
project_context: This ties into the design decision not to unnecessarily wrap small calculation, normalization, and validation helpers in classes.
reading_goal_internal: 함수 이름 add와 두 positional parameter a,b 및 들여쓴 반환 본문을 읽고, 이 작은 계산은 별도 객체 상태 없이 함수로 표현된 구조임을 이해한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `def name(parameters):` defines the name, input parameters, and body of a callable function.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Identify the function name following `def`, and check the number of parameters inside the parentheses and the boundary of the body below the colon.
concept_explanation.key_point: Expressing simple calculations as functions is standard Python design, and the absence of `self` or `class` does not constitute an error.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that reusable behavior in Python must be a method within a class.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Define a small calculation that requires only two inputs as a regular function, without using a class.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Identify that this is a function definition using the `def` keyword. 2) The function name is `add`. 3) The `a` and `b` inside the parentheses are the two parameters. 4) The indented `return` statement constitutes the body of the `add` function.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This statement correctly defines a general function `add` that takes two parameters.

common_wrong_choice.choice: There is no `self`, so this is a syntax error.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `self` is a parameter required by the conventions for instance methods, but it is not required for regular functions.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It’s easy to assume that reusable behavior in Python must be a method within a class.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Regardless of design choices, function definitions are read as **name → parameters → body → execution upon call**.

common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that `self.name` is a class variable shared by all `User` instances or that it is equivalent to a global variable named `name`.

title: `class Dog(Animal):` Specifying the parent class Animal

question: What is the role of `class Dog(Animal):` in `Animal`?
explanation: 1) The new class name following the `class` keyword is `Dog`. 2) The `Animal` class name appears inside the parentheses. 3) The `Animal` at this location specifies the base class of `Dog`. 4) Therefore, method lookup for `Dog` extends to `Animal` if necessary.
project_context: This relates to a structure in which common behaviors are placed in a parent class and reused by multiple child classes.
reading_goal_internal: class 헤더 괄호 안의 Animal이 Dog의 base class로 지정되어 상속 관계가 만들어지는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `class Child(Base):` defines a new class that inherits from `Base`.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Read the new class name following `class` and the base class name in parentheses separately, and make it clear that method lookup can extend all the way to the parent class.
concept_explanation.key_point: Even if the `Dog` class itself does not have a `speak` method, it can find the `speak` method in its parent class, `Animal`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think `Animal` is an ordinary function argument passed to the `Dog` constructor.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `Child` inherits from `Base`, you can use `Base`’s `value` method.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The new class name following the `class` keyword is `Dog`. 2) The `Animal` class name appears inside the parentheses. 3) The `Animal` at this location specifies the base class of `Dog`. 4) Therefore, method lookup for `Dog` extends to `Animal` if necessary.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The name in parentheses in the class definition header specifies the base class to be inherited from.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: An instance is created separately by calling `Dog()`, and `Animal` here is the base class in the class definition.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between class definition parentheses and function call parentheses based on context.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The inheritance header is read in the following order: **new class name → *base* in parentheses → class body**.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `def name(parameters):` creates a function definition in the current scope; if it appears within a class body, it becomes a method definition.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check whether a method with the same name exists in the parent class, but in this case, read “primary” as referring to the `def` header itself within the child class.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since there is a new `speak` definition inside `Dog`, this method is selected first when calling the `Dog` instance.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that using the same name means the parent method file itself has been deleted or modified.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The `Animal` class already has a `speak` method. 2) `Dog` inherits from `Animal`. 3) A `speak` method with the same name is also defined in the `Dog` class. 4) For a `Dog` instance, `Dog.speak` is found first and returns `bark`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the child class `Dog` contains a method definition with the same name, that definition is selected.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `sound` is the return value of the parent method `Animal.speak`, but `Dog` has a method with the same name that is more closely related.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: In method exploration, verify whether the child class definition comes first.

answer_explanation.takeaway: When reading about overrides, follow this order: **Check the parent method → Check for a def statement with the same name in the child → Give priority to the child’s definition**.

title: `super().__init__(name)` Executing Parent Initialization Logic via a Call
reading_goal: Read the flow where the parent navigation object provided by `super()` locates the `__init__` method, passes the `name` value, and executes the parent’s initialization code.
question: `super().__init__(name)` What is the final output after execution?
explanation: 1) The `Admin('Mina', 3)` call passes in the `name` and `level` values. 2) `super()` provides the path to call the parent’s initialization. 3) `__init__(name)` executes `User.__init__` and stores “Mina” in `self.name`. 4) The next line stores 3 in `self.level`, causing “Mina 3” to be printed.
project_context: This relates to inheritance code that reuses the parent’s common initialization logic while adding only child attributes.
reading_goal_internal: super()가 제공하는 부모 탐색 객체에서 __init__ 메서드를 찾아 name 값을 전달하고 부모의 초기화 코드를 실행하는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A method call in the form `object.method(arguments)` looks up and executes a method on the target object.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the result of ``super()``, then separate the ``__init__`` method call from that object and the argument `name`.
concept_explanation.key_point: The parent `User.__init__` is executed, so the `self.name` attribute is set first.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think that `super` is the parent class name itself or syntax for defining a new `__init__`.

teaching_example.walkthrough: When initializing a child object, call the parent’s `Base.__init__` to set the `name` attribute.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The `Admin('Mina', 3)` call passes in the `name` and `level` values. 2) `super()` provides the path to call the parent’s initialization. 3) `__init__(name)` executes `User.__init__` and stores “Mina” in `self.name`. 4) The next line stores 3 in `self.level`, causing “Mina 3” to be printed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The parent initialization call stores `name`, and the child initialization adds `level`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The parent’s `User.__init__` is actually executed, setting `self.name` to Mina.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Trace whether attribute assignments in the parent body are executed after a `super` call.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A `super` method call is interpreted as **selecting the parent path → finding the method → passing arguments → executing the parent’s body**.

title: `@dataclass` Applying a decorator to the class definition immediately below it
reading_goal: Read that the `@dataclass` decorator, located immediately above the class definition, is a decorator that creates a Card class object, converts it into a dataclass function, and then binds it back to the class name.
code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Card:
    title: str
    level: int

card = Card("list", 3)
print(card.title, card.level)
question: What does the `@dataclass` decorator apply to?
choices: The Card class definition is right below this.
answer: The Card class definition is right below this.
explanation: 1) The `from import` statement imports the `dataclass` name into the current scope. 2) The definition of the `Card` class is located immediately below the `@dataclass` line. 3) After the `Card` class is created, the `dataclass` conversion is applied. 4) As a result, you can use the constructor to receive field values, among other things.
project_context: This ties into the use of dataclasses to reduce repetitive initialization code for data-centric object models, such as cards, settings, and progress status.
reading_goal_internal: 클래스 정의 바로 위의 `@dataclass`가 Card 클래스 객체를 만들어진 뒤 dataclass 함수로 변환해 다시 이름에 연결하는 장식 문법임을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A class decorator is a syntax that applies a transformation function to a class created by placing `@decorator` before the class definition.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: @ Treat the line and the class definition immediately below it as a single unit, and identify which function the decorator name refers to.
concept_explanation.key_point: A `dataclass` can use field information to generate repetitive code, such as `__init__`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that @dataclass is a regular comment and therefore has no effect on execution.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The @mark decorator is applied to the Item class below to add a tag attribute.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The `from import` statement imports the `dataclass` name into the current scope. 2) The definition of the `Card` class is located immediately below the `@dataclass` line. 3) After the `Card` class is created, the `dataclass` conversion is applied. 4) As a result, you can use the constructor to receive field values, among other things.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The decorator syntax applies to the element being defined immediately following it—in this case, the Card class.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `title` is one of the class fields, and the decorator applies to the entire `Card` class definition.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: @ Consider the scope of the line and the definition immediately below it together.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A decorator is read as **check @name → check the definition immediately below → apply the transformation to the defined object**.

title: Creating a new object by calling `dataclass`Card(...)``
reading_goal: Read the flow where a constructor call invokes the class name to create a new instance, and the passed values are assigned to attributes.
code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Card:
    title: str
    level: int

card = Card("list basics", 3)
print(card.title)
question: What is the output of the `Card("list basics", 3)` property of the object created with `title`?
explanation: The `Card` class defines the `title` and `level` fields in that order. A new object is created with `list basics` as the first value passed to the constructor (`title`) and 3 as the second value (`level`). That object is stored in `card`, and `card.title` is `list basics`. If you map the constructor call arguments to the dataclass fields in order, the value of `title` is `list basics`. A common source of confusion: 3. 3 is the value assigned to the second field, `level`, but the question asks you to output the `title` attribute. Point of Misinterpretation: Reconcile the order of the constructor arguments with the order of the fields defined in the class. When you call the dataclass’s class name, a new instance is created, and the passed values are assigned to the fields.
project_context: The context involves understanding code that creates dataclass objects from structured data—such as study cards—and reads their fields.
reading_goal_internal: class 이름을 호출하는 constructor call이 새 instance를 만들고 전달한 값이 attribute에 연결되는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: Calling a class name with parentheses is a constructor call that creates a new object of that class. A dataclass is also a class, so it can create objects the same way.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: For `Card("list basics", 3)`, check the field order of `Card` and map each argument to the field it enters.
concept_explanation.key_point: `Card` is a class name, and `Card(...)` is a call that creates an object of that class. The created object is stored in the `card` variable.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to think that `Card("list basics", 3)` recreates the class definition itself. The class definition is read once at the top; this line is a call that creates a new instance based on that design.

teaching_example.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    age: int

user = User("Mina", 20)
print(user.age)
teaching_example.walkthrough: `User("Mina", 20)` creates a new User object, and since the second value, 20, is assigned to the age field, `user.age` is 20.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The `Card` class defines the `title` and `level` fields in that order. A new object is created with the first argument of the constructor—`list basics`—assigned to `title` and 3 assigned to `level`. That object is stored in `card`, and ``card.title`` is ``list basics``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: If you match the constructor call arguments with the dataclass fields in order, the value of `title` is `list basics`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 3 is the value entered in the second field, "level," and the problem outputs the "title" attribute.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Re-map the order of constructor arguments to the order of fields defined in the class.

answer_explanation.takeaway: When you call the `dataclass` class name, a new instance is created and the values you pass are assigned to the fields.

title: Grouping related data and actions together at `class Card`
reading_goal: Read the criteria for determining when to use a class when related data structures and behaviors recur.
question: If multiple cards repeatedly have `title`, `answer` data, and the `check_answer()` action, why is it a good idea to consider using `class Card:`?
choices: By grouping recurring related data and behaviors into a single structure, it can be reused across multiple objects, so
When you use `class`, all function calls automatically become faster, so
Since you cannot store variable values inside a class,
A class is only necessary when related data and behavior appear only once, so
answer: By grouping recurring related data and behaviors into a single structure, it can be reused across multiple objects, so
explanation: 1) Multiple cards share the same state type, “title/answer.” 2) The same action, “check_answer,” is repeated. 3) If you group this repetitive structure into a class, you can reuse the same behavior while varying the values for each instance. This explanation interprets the Python target for this card by linking it to legacy/domain objectives, noting that grouping repetitive related data and behavior into a single structure allows for reuse across multiple objects. A class should be considered when grouping **structures with recurring related data and behavior** for reuse.
project_context: This is the context for reading code structured as a class, where the same data and correct answer verification actions are repeated across multiple objects, similar to flashcards.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `class name:` is a Python statement that begins the definition of a new class. Within the indented block, you can define the data and behavior that the object will possess.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: When you encounter a `class` line, first check the class name, then look at the indented methods below it to see what state they store and what behavior they provide.
concept_explanation.key_point: The purpose of preserving this card is to highlight the design decision of **when to use `class`**, rather than the grammatical definition of `class Card:`.
